summary: Discusses and defines terms used when describing performance benchmark tests for network interconnection devices and their results. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: To compare network devices, buyers need everyone to measure speed and delay the same way. This memo defines those measuring words so vendors can report results that mean the same thing.

questions: how is latency defined for network devices
what is benchmarking terminology for network devices
subtitle: A shared vocabulary so vendors measure and report network device performance in comparable ways.

tldr.problem: Vendors of network devices often engage in specsmanship, reporting performance numbers in confusing ways that buyers cannot compare.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines 17 terms, including throughput, latency, frame loss rate and back-to-back, each with a definition, a discussion, measurement units, issues and cross references.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that sets up later memos to define specific tests and a reporting format. It is updated by RFC 6201.

facts.label: Back-to-back burst example
facts.value: A 64K-octet block split into many fragments

today: RFC 1242 is an Informational memo and is updated by RFC 6201. It defines terms only; the specific tests and reporting formats were left to follow-up memos.

sections.title: Why Benchmarking Terms Are Needed
sections.content:
RFC 1242 is a product of the Benchmarking Methodology Working Group (BMWG) of the IETF. It opens with a frank complaint: vendors often engage in specsmanship in an attempt to give their products a better position in the marketplace, usually through smoke and mirrors that confuse the user.

The memo and its follow-up memos try to define a specific set of terminology and tests that vendors can use to measure and report the performance characteristics of network devices. The goal is to give the user comparable data from different vendors with which to evaluate those devices.
sections.plainLanguage: If every shop measured speed its own way, buyers could not compare products. This memo agrees on the measuring words so the numbers can be compared.

sections.title: How Each Term Is Defined
sections.content:
Every term follows the same template: a Definition, a Discussion of the term and any restrictions on measurement, the Measurement units used to report it, a list of Issues that affect it, and a See Also list of related terms.

Some of the terms are about the kind of device being tested. A bridge is a system that forwards data frames based on information in the data link layer. A router forwards data frames based on information in the network layer, which implies running the network level routing algorithm and performing whatever actions the protocol requires, such as decrementing the TTL field in the TCP/IP header. A bridge/router can selectively act as a router or a bridge based on the protocol of a specific frame.
sections.plainLanguage: Each word gets the same small card: what it means, how to count it, what can spoil the reading, and which other words to look at.

sections.title: Frames, Load and Timing Terms
sections.content:
Several terms pin down exactly what is being counted. Data link frame size is the number of octets in the frame from the first octet after the preamble to the end of the FCS if one is present, or to the last octet of data if there is none. The memo notes that authors disagree about whether to include the checksum, so it sets one definition for this and later memos. Inter Frame Gap is the delay from the end of one data link frame to the start of the preamble of the next.

A Constant Load is fixed length frames at a fixed interval, and when a frame carries a checksum it must be verified. The memo admits that a steady load is rare in the real world but says measuring steady state performance can help compare competing devices. Back-to-back means fixed length frames sent at the minimum legal separation for the medium over a short to medium period, starting from an idle state, and is reported as the number of N-octet frames in a burst. It tests how much data buffering a device has; the memo gives examples such as a 64K-octet block from a remote disk server being split into many fragments, or routing updates that span many frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Before timing a runner you must agree where the line is. These words say exactly where a frame starts and ends, how tightly frames can be packed, and what a steady stream of frames means.

sections.title: Throughput, Loss and Latency
sections.content:
Throughput is the maximum rate at which none of the offered frames are dropped by the device. It is reported as N-octet input frames per second or input bits per second, measured over an assortment of frame sizes, with separate figures for routed and bridged data in devices that support both. If a received frame carries a checksum, full checksum processing must be done.

Frame Loss Rate is the percentage of frames that should have been forwarded under steady state load but were not, because of a lack of resources. It is reported as a graph of offered load against frame loss, and it can show how a device behaves in an overloaded state such as a broadcast storm.

Latency depends on the device type. For store and forward devices it runs from when the last bit of the input frame reaches the input port to when the first bit of the output frame is seen on the output port. For bit forwarding devices it runs from the end of the first input bit to the start of the first output bit. A cut through device that begins transmitting before the whole frame arrives is still treated as store and forward, so the measured latency can even be negative.
sections.plainLanguage: Throughput is how fast a device moves frames without dropping any. Frame loss rate is how many are dropped when it is pushed too far. Latency is how long a single frame takes to pass through.

sections.title: Behavior Under Stress and Change
sections.content:
The remaining terms describe behavior rather than a single number. Link Speed Mismatch is a mismatch between input and output data rates, such as an Ethernet on one side and a 56KB serial link on the other, also called the fire hose effect. MTU-mismatch behavior covers an output network whose MTU is smaller than the input network's, which forces fragmentation. Overhead behavior is processing done other than for normal data frames, such as handling routing updates or responding to network management requests. Overloaded behavior is what happens when demand exceeds available system resources, and any frame loss is taken as an overloaded state.

Further terms are Policy based filtering, discarding received frames by administrative decision where normal operation would forward them; Restart behavior, the reinitialization of a system causing data loss, measured as the period after a power up or reset when the device does not accept and forward frames; and Single frame behavior, one frame received in isolation, which can take much longer than the same frame inside a steady stream because of work such as figuring routes, performing ARPs and setting up cache entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tests ask how a device acts when things go wrong: when it is rebooting, when it is swamped, when a filter blocks traffic, or when the very first frame arrives before anything is ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states only that security issues are not discussed in it. RFC 1242 defines vocabulary; it does not specify a protocol or an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is only a list of measuring words, so it says nothing about security.
